RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Aminata Diallo is a young woman living in a rented room in a bustling district on the outskirts of Bamako, in a setting of packed-earth walls, corrugated tin roofing, no tap water, and daily dependence on a communal stand for water. She rises before dawn and works six days a week on a construction site as a masonry laborer. She is the youngest person on the crew and the only woman. Her master mason, Sékou, an older man who lost two fingers to a faulty crane, calls her la petite comptable because she repeatedly recalculates load-bearing estimates in her head and checks measurements carefully before working. He has begun checking her arithmetic before approving estimates, which signals quiet trust. Aminata is also an accounting student, saving for classes at a community center on the other side of the city. She cannot afford bus fare both ways, so she often walks. She sends monthly remittances to her younger sister, who depends on them, and she is saving to house her sister and support her schooling.

Her values center on careful accounting, self-reliance, and saving against hardship. She carries a small notebook tucked inside her shirt for figures and dates, and she keeps an emergency fund hidden under a loose floorboard near her mattress. She deposits the same amount each month and does not touch it or count it in daylight. She is frugal, disciplined, and keeps her plans private. She does not speak openly about hopes or long-term plans, in part because she believes plans discussed aloud become vulnerable to being borrowed against. Her practical habits are shaped by a strong need to double-check costs, quantities, and measurements, and she routinely counts bricks, rice costs, steps, and weeks until exams. She is highly self-monitoring, precise, cautious, and reserved, and she responds to teasing with silence or a nod rather than talkativeness.

Her family history strongly informs her habits. Her mother lost a market stall after a miscalculated loan, and this taught Aminata to verify figures carefully. Her mother died when Aminata was twelve. Her father later sold his tools to pay for a funeral and never held a trowel again, leaving a lasting lesson that material security can disappear quickly. These experiences are tied to her tendency to count, track, save, and avoid unnecessary spending. She works long hours doing manual labor, has limited money, and manages the practical constraints of low income, distance, and physical fatigue while maintaining her studies and remittances.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

It is Friday evening. Aminata is walking home from the construction site as the air cools and the street fills with people. She passes a tea vendor she sees every Friday. The vendor sets up near the corner, and the smell of ginger and mint drifts toward her. She has exact coins in one pocket for a small cup of tea, which she rarely allows herself, and in the other pocket she has the bus ticket she saved by walking to work that morning. If she took the bus, she would get home before dark and have more time to study before her eyes grow too tired. She stops briefly and looks at the vendor and then at the empty street stretching toward home.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

She is physically tired: her shoulders ache from carrying cement bags, and her feet are blistered from the day’s work. She is thirsty, though not severely so, and the smell of tea is appealing. She is aware that darkness will fall in about forty minutes and that the walk home takes thirty. Her immediate sensory cues include the ginger-and-mint scent from the tea stall and the evening street noise as people gather.

The scent of tea brings forward an accessible memory of her mother brewing tea on a Friday evening after a long week at the market. The bus ticket in her pocket cues the memory of choosing to walk instead of using it that morning so it would be available now. These are directly cued memories associated with the present objects and smells, rather than reflective recollections. Her recent pattern is also relevant: she has skipped the tea stop on at least four Fridays this month, pocketing the coins each time, and she has walked to work every morning this week despite having bus fare saved. She has never taken the bus home on a Friday, preferring to save the ticket for a weekday when she is more tired.
